name: Grand-Place
why_interesting: Rebuilt spectacularly after Louis XIV’s 1695 bombardment; the guildhall ensemble is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

name: Brussels Town Hall
why_interesting: Construction began in 1401; its soaring 15th-century tower was completed by Jan van Ruysbroeck and remains Brussels’ civic landmark.

name: Maison du Roi / Brussels City Museum
why_interesting: The neo-Gothic Maison du Roi was rebuilt in the late 19th century and has housed Brussels’ city museum since 1887.

name: Maison des Ducs de Brabant
why_interesting: Seven guildhouses hide behind one monumental Baroque façade, designed by Guillaume de Bruyn during the Grand-Place rebuilding of 1698.

name: Le Pigeon (De Duif) Guildhouse
why_interesting: Rebuilt in 1697 after the bombardment; Victor Hugo lived here in 1852 while exiled from France.

name: Le Cygne (De Zwaan) Guildhouse
why_interesting: Rebuilt after the 1695 bombardment, this Grand-Place guildhouse later became a meeting place frequented by Karl Marx in the 1840s.

name: Maison des Brasseurs / Brewers’ House
why_interesting: Rebuilt in 1698 by Guillaume de Bruyn for the brewers’ guild, it remains a showpiece of Brussels’ beer heritage.

name: Everard ’t Serclaes Monument
why_interesting: Julien Dillens created this 1898 memorial to Everard ’t Serclaes, the 14th-century hero who helped recover Brussels from Flemish occupation.

name: Royal Saint-Hubert Galleries
why_interesting: Opened in 1847 to designs by Jean-Pierre Cluysenaar, these glass-roofed galleries rank among Europe’s earliest purpose-built shopping arcades.

name: Royal Theatre Toone
why_interesting: Brussels’ Toone puppet tradition dates to around 1830, when Antoine ‘Toone’ Genty established a popular marionette theatre.

name: Saint Nicholas Church
why_interesting: A church has stood here since the 12th century; the present building survived repeated rebuilding, including after the devastating 1695 bombardment.

name: Manneken Pis
why_interesting: The famous bronze fountain statue was made in 1619 by Jérôme Duquesnoy the Elder and now has a wardrobe of hundreds of costumes.

name: A la Mort Subite
why_interesting: Its curious name dates to around 1910 under Théophile Vossen; the wonderfully preserved café interior largely dates from 1928.

name: Au Bon Vieux Temps
why_interesting: Hidden down an old alley beside Saint Nicholas Church, this intimate heritage tavern is prized for its vaulted interior and stained glass.

name: Brussels Stock Exchange (Bourse)
why_interesting: Inaugurated in 1873, this monumental exchange was designed by Léon-Pierre Suys and Jules Brunfaut and now houses Belgian Beer World.

name: Bruxella 1238
why_interesting: Archaeological remains beneath the city centre preserve a Franciscan convent founded in 1238, revealing medieval Brussels below today’s streets.

name: Café Le Cirio
why_interesting: Open since 1886, this richly preserved café retains Belle Époque and Art Nouveau details from Brussels’ great age of grand brasseries.

name: Le Falstaff
why_interesting: Created in 1903, its exuberant Art Nouveau interior was decorated by Émile Houbion, a collaborator of Victor Horta.

name: Brasserie Greenwich
why_interesting: A listed Belle Époque tavern from the early 20th century, remembered as a chess haunt of surrealist René Magritte and Paul Nougé.

name: Halles Saint-Géry
why_interesting: Built in 1881 as an indoor market hall on the traditional birthplace of Brussels, it now hosts exhibitions, events and nightlife.

name: L’Archiduc
why_interesting: Opened in 1937 and turned into a jazz club by Stan Brenders in 1953; Miles Davis and Nat King Cole are among its legendary associations.

name: Anneessens Tower
why_interesting: One of the best-preserved remnants of Brussels’ first defensive wall, built in the early 13th century around the medieval city.

name: Villers Tower and First City Wall
why_interesting: These surviving towers and wall fragments date from Brussels’ first fortifications, erected in the early 13th century.

name: La Monnaie / De Munt
why_interesting: The present opera house opened in 1819; an 1830 performance of Auber’s La Muette de Portici helped ignite the Belgian Revolution.

name: Martyrs’ Square
why_interesting: Laid out in 1774 by Claude Fisco; its crypt honours 466 people killed during the Belgian Revolution of 1830.

name: Black Tower
why_interesting: This sturdy 13th-century tower is a rare survivor of Brussels’ first city wall, now dramatically enclosed by later urban development.

name: Saint Catherine Church
why_interesting: Built from 1854 to 1874 on the former harbour basin, this striking church marks the transformation of Brussels’ old port district.

name: Church of Saint John the Baptist at the Béguinage
why_interesting: The present 17th-century Baroque church replaced an earlier Gothic church serving a beguinage that once contained more than 1,000 houses.

name: Grand Hospice
why_interesting: Built in 1824-1827 to plans by Henri Partoes, this vast neoclassical hospice once cared for Brussels’ sick and elderly.

name: Maison de la Bellone
why_interesting: Its spectacular Baroque courtyard façade was carved in 1697 by Jean Cosyn, architect-sculptor also involved in rebuilding the Grand-Place.

name: In ’t Spinnekopke
why_interesting: Set in an 18th-century house reputedly used as a stagecoach stop, this old estaminet specialises in Belgian beer and traditional dishes.

name: Grand Sablon
why_interesting: A medieval sandy market space transformed into an aristocratic quarter, today framed by the 15th-century Sablon church and historic mansions.

name: Petit Sablon
why_interesting: Inaugurated in 1890, Henri Beyaert’s neo-Renaissance garden features statues of the Counts of Egmont and Hornes and 48 historic Brussels guilds.

name: Church of Our Lady of Victories at the Sablon
why_interesting: This magnificent 15th-century Gothic church grew from the crossbow guild’s chapel and is closely linked to Brussels’ historic Ommegang procession.

name: Egmont Palace
why_interesting: Built in stages from the 16th century for the Counts of Egmont and later the Arenberg family, it now hosts Belgian diplomatic receptions.

name: Egmont Park
why_interesting: In the 16th century the park and palace belonged to Princess Françoise de Luxembourg, widow of Count Jean d’Egmont.

name: Palace of Justice
why_interesting: Joseph Poelaert’s colossal courthouse was built from 1866 to 1883 under Leopold II and remains one of Brussels’ most imposing landmarks.

name: Poelaert Square
why_interesting: Created beside Joseph Poelaert’s 19th-century Palace of Justice, the square now offers one of the city’s broadest panoramic viewpoints.

name: Place du Jeu de Balle
why_interesting: Brussels’ famous flea market has traded here since 1873; Hergé later immortalised it in Tintin’s The Secret of the Unicorn.

name: Church of Our Lady of the Chapel
why_interesting: With origins in the 12th century, this Gothic church is where Pieter Bruegel the Elder married and was buried in 1569.

name: Church of Saints John and Stephen of the Minimes
why_interesting: Built for the Minim friars in the early 18th century; Renaissance anatomist Andreas Vesalius is traditionally associated with the neighbouring street.

name: Brigittines Chapel
why_interesting: This 1663 Baroque convent chapel now stands beside Andrea Bruno’s contemporary extension and serves as a distinctive performing-arts venue.

name: Halle Gate
why_interesting: A surviving 14th-century gate of Brussels’ second city wall, dramatically recast in neo-Gothic style by architect Henri Beyaert in the 19th century.

name: Jewish Museum of Belgium
why_interesting: Established in 1990, the museum explores Jewish history, religion and culture in Belgium through objects, testimony and changing exhibitions.

name: La Fleur en Papier Doré
why_interesting: This listed 17th-century tavern became a favourite meeting place of René Magritte, Marcel Mariën, Louis Scutenaire and CoBrA artists.

name: Royal Palace of Brussels
why_interesting: The present palace began taking shape in the 1820s; Leopold II gave its monumental façade its current appearance in the early 1900s.

name: Place Royale
why_interesting: This harmonious late-18th-century neoclassical square replaced part of the ruined Coudenberg palace complex and centres on Godfrey of Bouillon’s 1848 statue.

name: Church of Saint James on Coudenberg
why_interesting: Begun in 1776 as part of Place Royale’s neoclassical ensemble, this temple-like church dominates Brussels’ historic seat of royal power.

name: Coudenberg Palace Archaeological Site
why_interesting: The buried remains reveal the palace where Charles V assumed power in 1515 and abdicated in 1555, before fire destroyed it in 1731.

name: BELvue Museum
why_interesting: Housed in the former Hôtel Bellevue, built in 1776 beside the Royal Palace, this museum traces Belgium’s history and national identity.

name: Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium
why_interesting: Founded in 1801, Belgium’s national fine-arts collection spans Bruegel, Rubens and later masters across six interconnected museums.

name: Magritte Museum
why_interesting: Opened in 2009, it houses the world’s largest collection devoted to Belgian surrealist René Magritte, with around 230 works and archives.

name: Musical Instruments Museum (Old England)
why_interesting: The museum’s collection dates to 1877; since 2000 it has filled Paul Saintenoy’s spectacular 1899 Old England Art Nouveau department store.

name: Palace of Charles of Lorraine
why_interesting: This elegant 18th-century residence belonged to Charles Alexander of Lorraine, popular governor of the Austrian Netherlands from 1744 to 1780.

name: Mont des Arts
why_interesting: First landscaped for the 1910 international exhibition and rebuilt in the 1950s, this cultural hill links medieval lower Brussels with the royal quarter.

name: Academy Palace
why_interesting: Built in 1823-1828 as a residence for the Prince of Orange, it has housed Belgium’s Royal Academies since 1876.

name: Palace of the Nation
why_interesting: Built in 1783 by Barnabé Guimard for the Council of Brabant, this neoclassical palace became the home of Belgium’s parliament after independence.

name: Brussels Park
why_interesting: Laid out in the late 18th century on the former ducal hunting park, it became a battleground during the Belgian Revolution of 1830.

name: BOZAR / Centre for Fine Arts
why_interesting: Victor Horta designed this landmark arts centre between 1922 and 1929, adapting his modern architecture to a difficult sloping city-centre site.

name: Cathedral of St Michael and St Gudula
why_interesting: Construction began in 1226; its Brabant Gothic interior includes major 16th-century stained glass associated with Charles V and the Habsburg court.

name: Church of Our Lady of Finistere
why_interesting: The present Baroque church dates from 1730 and contains a dramatic black carved pulpit of 1758 depicting the Fall of Man.

name: Congress Column
why_interesting: Erected in 1850-1859 to Joseph Poelaert’s design, the column honours Belgium’s 1831 constitution and is crowned by a statue of Leopold I.

name: Cinquantenaire Park
why_interesting: Created in 1880 for the 50th anniversary of Belgian independence, the park became Leopold II’s grand showcase of national ambition.

name: Cinquantenaire Arch
why_interesting: Completed in 1905 under Leopold II, Charles Girault’s monumental triumphal arch crowned the grand Cinquantenaire ensemble begun for Belgium’s 1880 jubilee.

name: Art & History Museum
why_interesting: Belgium’s national antiquities collections trace their roots to 1835; the Cinquantenaire museum ranges from prehistory and Egypt to medieval tapestries.

name: Royal Museum of the Armed Forces and Military History
why_interesting: Founded in 1910 and moved to the Cinquantenaire in 1923, it displays armour, aircraft and military history from medieval times onward.

name: Autoworld
why_interesting: Opened in 1986 inside a former 1880 exhibition hall, Autoworld showcases a major collection charting automotive design from the pioneering era onward.

name: Leopold Park
why_interesting: Created as a zoological garden in the 19th century, it later became a scientific campus and now forms a green heart of the European Quarter.

name: Solvay Library
why_interesting: Built in 1902 as part of industrialist Ernest Solvay’s ambitious scientific campus, this richly decorated library remains a jewel of Leopold Park.

name: Wiertz Museum
why_interesting: Romantic painter Antoine Wiertz had this monumental studio built in 1850; after his death it became one of Belgium’s earliest artist museums.

name: House of European History (Eastman Building)
why_interesting: The museum occupies Michel Polak’s 1930s Eastman Dental Institute, funded by Kodak founder George Eastman and repurposed for European history.

name: Hôtel van Eetvelde
why_interesting: Victor Horta designed this revolutionary Art Nouveau townhouse from 1895 for diplomat Edmond van Eetvelde; it is now UNESCO-listed.

name: Maison Saint-Cyr
why_interesting: Built in 1901-1903 by Gustave Strauven for painter Georges de Saint-Cyr, its four-metre-wide façade is an exuberant Art Nouveau landmark.

name: Horta Museum
why_interesting: Victor Horta built his own home and studio here in 1898-1901; the UNESCO-listed interior is one of the purest Art Nouveau experiences in Brussels.

name: Saint-Gilles Town Hall
why_interesting: Built in 1900-1904 by Albert Dumont, this neo-Renaissance town hall contains decoration by leading Belgian Symbolists including Fernand Khnopff.

name: Brasserie Verschueren
why_interesting: Founded in 1880 by Louis-François Verschueren, this classic neighbourhood café preserves old signage and generations of Saint-Gilles social history.

name: Hôtel Solvay
why_interesting: Victor Horta designed this lavish UNESCO-listed townhouse for industrialist Armand Solvay between 1894 and 1903, with interiors conceived as a total work of art.

name: Hôtel Tassel
why_interesting: Designed by Victor Horta for scientist Émile Tassel in 1893, this UNESCO-listed house is widely considered a foundational masterpiece of Art Nouveau.

name: Maison Ciamberlani
why_interesting: Paul Hankar designed this dramatic 1897 townhouse for Symbolist painter Albert Ciamberlani, with an extraordinary façade dominated by sweeping sgraffito decoration.

name: Maison Hankar
why_interesting: Architect Paul Hankar built this as his own house in 1893, making it one of Brussels’ earliest and most personal Art Nouveau statements.

name: Flagey Building
why_interesting: Joseph Diongre built this streamlined Art Deco broadcasting headquarters in 1935-1938; its ship-like form earned it the nickname ‘the Packet Boat’.

name: La Cambre Abbey
why_interesting: Founded around 1201 for Cistercian nuns, this former abbey was rebuilt in the 17th and 18th centuries and retains tranquil historic gardens.

name: Saint Boniface Church
why_interesting: Built in 1846-1849 by Joseph Jonas Dumont, this pioneering neo-Gothic church helped define the later Saint-Boniface neighbourhood of Ixelles.

name: Villa Empain / Boghossian Foundation
why_interesting: Michel Polak designed this luxurious Art Deco villa in 1930 for 21-year-old Baron Louis Empain; today it hosts the Boghossian Foundation.

name: Autrique House
why_interesting: Built in 1893 for engineer Eugène Autrique, this was Victor Horta’s first major townhouse and an important step toward mature Art Nouveau.

name: Schaerbeek Town Hall
why_interesting: Jules-Jacques van Ysendyck’s Flemish neo-Renaissance town hall opened in 1887; after a 1911 arson attack, his son Maurice rebuilt it.

name: Maison des Arts de Schaerbeek
why_interesting: Built in 1826 for the Eenens family, this former private mansion became Schaerbeek’s Maison des Arts after the commune acquired it in 1950.

name: Schaerbeek Station / Train World
why_interesting: The historic station complex developed from the late 19th century; since 2015 it has formed the atmospheric gateway to Belgium’s Train World museum.

name: Atomium
why_interesting: Created for Expo 58 by engineer André Waterkeyn and architects André and Jean Polak, it represents an iron crystal enlarged 165 billion times.

name: Royal Greenhouses of Laeken
why_interesting: Alphonse Balat designed the first greenhouse in 1873 for Leopold II; the vast glass-and-iron complex was developed between 1874 and 1905.

name: Church of Our Lady of Laeken
why_interesting: Commissioned by Leopold I after Queen Louise-Marie’s death in 1850, Joseph Poelaert’s neo-Gothic church was completed under Leopold II in 1909.

name: Laeken Cemetery
why_interesting: Developed beside the royal church in the 19th century, Brussels’ grand cemetery contains monuments to architect Joseph Poelaert, Alphonse Balat and singer Maria Malibran.

name: Erasmus House
why_interesting: Humanist Desiderius Erasmus stayed in this early-16th-century house in 1521 while working on his influential edition of the New Testament.

name: Anderlecht Beguinage
why_interesting: Founded in 1252, this tiny beguinage survives as two historic wings around an enclosed garden and is among Belgium’s smallest.

name: Collegiate Church of Saints Peter and Guidon
why_interesting: Its Romanesque origins reach the late 11th century; the later Gothic church grew around the cult and pilgrimage of local Saint Guidon.

name: Cantillon Brewery / Brussels Museum of the Gueuze
why_interesting: Founded in 1900, this family brewery still makes lambic and gueuze by traditional spontaneous fermentation using historic brewing equipment.

name: La Fonderie / Brussels Museum of Industry and Labour
why_interesting: The museum occupies the former Compagnie des Bronzes foundry, active from 1854 to 1979, preserving Brussels’ industrial and working-class heritage.

name: Church of Saint John the Baptist, Molenbeek
why_interesting: Joseph Diongre built this striking reinforced-concrete Art Deco church in 1932-1935, giving industrial Molenbeek one of Brussels’ boldest modern churches.

name: National Basilica of the Sacred Heart
why_interesting: Leopold II laid the foundation stone in 1905; Albert Van Huffel’s vast Art Deco basilica evolved over decades and was completed in 1970.

name: Van Buuren Museum and Gardens
why_interesting: Built in 1928 for collectors David and Alice van Buuren, this Art Deco home preserves original interiors, paintings and celebrated landscaped gardens.
